craft_claim: When bleakness becomes an end in itself—darkness without causal or moral pressure—it degrades into grimdark posturing: shock, nihilism-as-decoration, and misery that absolves rather than implicates.

supporting_evidence.location: Get Started in Writing Science Fiction and Fantasy, p. 42
supporting_evidence.note: Roberts characterises grimdark as fiction where nobody is honourable and might is right, and notes it conveys the sense that the world is a cynical, ultraviolent place rather than re-imagining any actual history.

Bourke identifies grimdark's defining risk as a retreat into valorising darkness for its own sake, a nihilism in which right action is impossible or futile—which absolves protagonist and reader of moral responsibility.
Walter criticises the trend as escalation (more fighting, bloodier blood) driven by a commercial imperative, set against more emotionally nuanced fantasy.

counterevidence.note: Section G bounds the failure to register without history: Roberts' definition targets fiction conveying a cynical, ultraviolent world rather than re-imagining any actual history, so darkness grounded in an examined history or indictment falls outside it and 'an end in itself' cannot be diagnosed from surface bleakness alone.

scope: Speculative fiction primarily, but the pattern generalises to any genre that uses bleakness as brand.
exceptions: Darkness may be the legitimate subject when it is causally and morally examined (for example atrocity as historical indictment); the failure is darkness as style.
